justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over longer horizons. For the one-day estimate of 63.85, I was primarily anchoring to the most recent price or index level and assuming mean-reverting behavior with minimal overnight drift — essentially projecting that the next session would close very close to where the prior one ended, with only a slight directional bias. For the one-week estimate of 64.10, I incorporated a small positive trend component, reflecting either a modest bullish bias in recent momentum or a slight upward drift assumption built into the underlying model. For the one-month estimate of 64.50, the continued modest upward drift reflects a baseline assumption of gradual appreciation consistent with long-run average returns or fundamental fair value, though the magnitude of the move remains subdued, suggesting I saw no strong catalyst driving a sharp directional move.

The confidence interval widths naturally expand as the time horizon extends, reflecting the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly 62.2 to 65.5 is quite tight, consistent with typical daily volatility for a moderately volatile asset or index. At one week, the interval widens to 60.5–67.7, capturing a broader range of possible paths over five trading sessions. By one month, the interval of 57.0–72.0 reflects the reality that many unpredictable developments — macro data, earnings, policy shifts, geopolitical events — can accumulate and compound over several weeks.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include a sudden shift in central bank policy signaling, an unexpected inflation or employment print that dramatically reprices rate expectations, or a geopolitical shock such as an escalation in an ongoing conflict or a trade policy surprise. On the upside, a better-than-expected earnings season or a dovish policy pivot could push prices well above the upper bound of the one-month interval. On the downside, a credit event, liquidity crisis, or sharp risk-off episode could easily breach the lower bound of 57.0.

It is also worth noting that tail risks are inherently underrepresented in symmetric confidence intervals like these. Real-world return distributions tend to exhibit fat tails and occasional sharp discontinuities — flash crashes, gap openings, or sudden sentiment reversals — that a normally-distributed model would assign very low probability to but which occur more frequently in practice. Readers should treat the stated intervals as reasonable central-tendency guides rather than hard bounds on possible outcomes.
